statement: A student predicts that in approach 4 the second transaction, seeing that the first row is being updated by the first thread, goes and queries the second row and updates that instead; the teacher asks why it would wait on the first row and then defers the question ('let me not dive into that').
detail: No verdict at this point. The teacher then asks the class whether the second transaction would wait on the first row or just move to the second row (00:52:50); the same student then reverses to 'it will wait' (K1-097). The mechanism is explained at 01:01:25 (K1-112/K1-113): waiting transactions re-evaluate the query after the lock holder commits.

statement: With SKIP LOCKED, when a transaction holding a row fails, the waiting transactions re-evaluate the statement and the next one gets the first free row because the query orders by ID; even without ORDER BY it would still match some free row.
detail: Part of the answer on whether a row released by a failed transaction is lost under SKIP LOCKED; the ordering by ID is why the released row is picked up first.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it re-evaluated statement, now it would get the first row because we are ordering by ID.
